Values and Preferences on the Use of Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP): A Systematic Review of the Literature Background: To date, two recommendations on the use of PrEP have been released by the World Health Organization (WHO). The first recommendation, released in 2012, was for serodiscordant couples, men, and transgender women who have sex with men, in the context of demonstration projects. A second recommendation for men who have sex with men (MSM) was released in 2014 as part of the WHO ARV guidelines, suggesting the use of PrEP as an additional tool within the realm of combination prevention. Following a large stakeholder consultation led by WHO in March 2015, a decision was made to consider including a recommendation on the use of PrEP for all populations at significant risk of HIV, as part of the WHO ARV guidance update to be released in 2015. This review of the values and preferences on PrEP of populations at substantial risk of acquiring HIV was mandated by WHO as part of the process of reviewing the overall evidence on PrEP. It was conducted by Florence Koechlin with the support of Ginny Fonner and Sarah Dalglish in the context of their work in systematic review of the evidence on PrEP. Method: A systematic review of articles and conference abstracts reporting on PrEP acceptability was embedded into the GRADE review. Data from those articles and abstracts were coded and entered into a spreadsheet. Findings were categorized by population groups (e.g., women, men, young women and adolescent girls, female sex workers, serodiscordant couples, people who inject drugs, transgender people), country/region, study size, and specific themes (e.g., awareness, willingness to use PrEP, barriers/facilitators, dosing/route of administration/dispensing facility, risk compensation, adherence). Other values and preferences reviews and consultation reports were also considered to verify consistency of findings. Overall themes reflecting common values and preferences across populations were first extracted from those articles. Findings specific to particular groups were then identified through qualitative grouping and analysis. Findings: The number of studies evaluating the acceptability of PrEP has grown exponentially among all populations since the first time PrEP was considered for recommendations by WHO in 2012. A total of 131 peer-reviewed articles and 46 abstracts were included for this review, totaling 177 references. Studies have a very wide geographical coverage across all continents. Findings reflecting the views of a clear majority of respondents or most of the population groups are listed in the section Overall Themes. Themes: The themes highlighted in this section reflect common values and preferences expressed across populations.
